blocks.prompt: The Ice Cream That Never Freezes Solid
blocks.text: Ice cream feels soft, but a freezer is cold enough to turn water into hard ice. So why can you scoop it? The secret is sugar. Sugar mixed into milk stops it from freezing all the way. Even in the freezer, tiny bits of the ice cream stay wet. Those wet bits let your spoon push through. There is a second secret. While ice cream is being made, a paddle spins and spins. The paddle whips air into the cream. Air makes it fluffy and light. A big scoop is almost one third air. So a scoop of ice cream is ice, sugar, milk, and a lot of air.

blocks.prompt: Why Old Ice Cream Gets Crunchy
blocks.text: Take a spoonful of fresh ice cream and it feels smooth, almost like cream. But that smoothness is a trick. Ice cream is full of ice crystals. There are millions of them in every bite. They feel smooth because they are tiny. Your tongue cannot feel an ice crystal smaller than about the width of a hair. Making them that small takes work. In an ice cream machine, a metal blade called a dasher scrapes the freezing mixture off the cold wall, over and over. Nothing gets a chance to freeze into a big lump. Tiny crystals form instead, and the ice cream comes out smooth. Now think about the tub at the back of your freezer. Every time the door opens, the ice cream warms a little. Some of the smallest crystals melt. When it cools down again, that melted water freezes onto the crystals that are left, making them bigger. Do that enough times and the crystals grow big enough for your tongue to notice. The ice cream turns gritty and crunchy. It is not spoiled. It is just no longer tiny.

blocks.prompt: Half of It Is Air
blocks.text: Pick up two pints of ice cream at the store and one will feel noticeably heavier than the other. Same size box, same flavor, different weight. The difference is air. Air is not a filler that got sneaked in. It is an ingredient, and ice cream does not work without it. As the mixture freezes, a spinning dasher whips air into it, breaking it into millions of bubbles so small you cannot see them. Those bubbles do two jobs. They keep the ice crystals apart, which is what makes ice cream feel creamy instead of like a block of frozen milk. They also insulate it, so a scoop warms slowly on your tongue instead of hitting you all at once. Ice cream makers have a word for how much air went in: overrun. If a gallon of liquid mixture comes out as two gallons of ice cream, that is one hundred percent overrun, and half of what you bought is air. Cheap ice cream sits near that limit. Premium brands use much less, sometimes only twenty percent, which is why a small tub of the good stuff feels like a brick. The United States government put a floor under this. To be sold as ice cream, the product must weigh at least four and a half pounds per gallon and contain at least ten percent milkfat. Fall below that and it has to be called something else, like frozen dairy dessert. Read the tubs in the freezer aisle and you will find both names sitting side by side. So when you buy ice cream, you are buying air. The trick is that you want to.

blocks.prompt: How to Freeze Something Before Freezers Existed
blocks.text: Ice cream has a problem that had to be solved before it could exist. To freeze cream you need something colder than freezing, and for most of human history nobody had anything that cold on purpose. Ice itself is not enough. A bucket of ice sits at thirty two degrees Fahrenheit, which is exactly the temperature at which water turns to ice. Pack a can of cream inside it and the cream will get cold and stay liquid. Something has to pull the temperature lower. The answer turned out to be salt, and it is one of the most useful pieces of kitchen chemistry ever found. Salt dissolves into the thin film of water on the surface of ice. Salty water freezes at a lower temperature than plain water, so the ice keeps melting even though it is already cold. Melting takes energy, and that energy has to come from somewhere. It comes out of everything nearby. A bucket of ice and salt can drop to about minus six degrees Fahrenheit, far below the freezing point of cream. Nobody planned this. Writers in India described cooling water with saltpeter around the twelve hundreds. By the fifteen hundreds the method had reached Europe, where a doctor in Rome wrote instructions for chilling wine with it. Cooks noticed that if a bucket could freeze water, it could freeze a sweetened cream too, and Italian and French kitchens began turning out frozen creams in the sixteen hundreds. It was rich food. It took ice hauled from mountains, stored in deep pits through the summer, and a servant willing to stir a can by hand for an hour. In eighteen forty three an American named Nancy Johnson patented the machine that made it ordinary: a bucket for ice and salt, a can for the cream, and a crank that turned a paddle inside. The paddle mattered more than the crank. It scraped freezing cream off the cold metal before it could set into a lump, which kept the ice crystals small and the texture smooth. Every modern ice cream machine still does exactly what Johnson's did. The refrigeration is electric now instead of salty, but there is still a cold wall and a paddle scraping it clean.

6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Ice Cream That Never Freezes Solid

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: A foam, an emulsion, and a suspension at once
About a fifth of the water never freezes
Guar and locust bean gum slow the damage
Grit begins around fifty micrometers
Cold blunts the receptors that taste sweetness
Brain freeze: sphenopalatine ganglioneuralgia

blocks.prompt: The Most Complicated Thing in Your Freezer
blocks.text: Ice cream looks simple. It is not. Food scientists describe it as three different physical systems occupying the same spoonful at the same time, and each one is doing a job. It is a foam, because roughly a third to a half of its volume is air, whipped in during freezing and trapped as bubbles too small to see. It is an emulsion, because microscopic droplets of butterfat hang suspended in water that would otherwise refuse to mix with them. And it is a suspension, because millions of ice crystals float in the mixture, held apart from one another by the fat and the bubbles. Take any one of the three away and you do not get worse ice cream. You get something that is not ice cream at all. The strangest part is what the freezer never manages to do. A home freezer sits near zero degrees Fahrenheit, cold enough to turn a glass of water into solid rock. It does not do that to ice cream. Sugar is the reason. Dissolved sugar lowers the freezing point of the water it sits in, and as the water around it turns to ice, the sugar that is left behind gets crowded into less and less liquid. The syrup grows more concentrated, its freezing point sinks lower, and the process stalls. Even after hours in the freezer, something like a fifth to a quarter of the water in ice cream is still liquid, a thick sugar syrup clinging between the ice crystals. That syrup is why a spoon goes in. Ice cream is scoopable because it never finishes freezing. Manufacturers spend real effort defending that structure. Gums such as guar and locust bean are added in quantities under half a percent, not for flavor but to thicken the unfrozen syrup so water molecules cannot travel easily. Traveling water is the enemy. Every time a tub warms slightly, the smallest ice crystals melt, and when it cools again that water freezes onto larger crystals rather than rebuilding the small ones. The crystals creep upward in size, and once they pass roughly fifty micrometers the tongue registers them as grit. This is why ice cream that has ridden home in a warm car and gone back in the freezer is never quite right again. Even your sense of taste is being manipulated. The receptors that detect sweetness work poorly at low temperature, which means ice cream tastes far less sweet cold than it actually is. Melt a premium vanilla in a bowl and drink it and the sugar is almost unpleasant. Manufacturers sweeten to the temperature at which the food will be eaten, not to the temperature at which it is mixed. And then there is the headache. Swallow something very cold very fast and it chills the roof of your mouth. Blood vessels there constrict, then flood open again, and a nerve bundle behind your nose misreports that whole event as pain coming from your forehead. Doctors call it sphenopalatine ganglioneuralgia. You call it brain freeze, and you can end it by pressing your tongue flat against the roof of your mouth and warming the spot back up. Simple food. Roughly four ingredients. It took chemistry, refrigeration, and about four hundred years of tinkering to make a thing that melts correctly on a tongue.
